To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“The discursive confusion that consumers face when trying to make sustainable consumption practices more mainstream, is caused by the simultaneous existence of multiple and partly clashing sustainable consumption discourses, as well as the continuous discursive struggle that arises from the discursive polyphonic nature of sustainable consumption discourses”.
consumers face a discursive confusion when trying to make sustainable consumption choices.
the knowledge-to-action gap in sustainable consumption is partly explained by the discursive confusion and discursive struggle that is inherent in the discursive polyphonic marketplace.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how consumers deal with discursive polyphony and the associated discursive struggles that arise from competing discourses in their daily life.
the discursive nature of marketplace knowledge, the implications of which for consumer policy and research are discussed.
the discursive confusion of consumers in their everyday lives and how this discursive polyphony affects consumers’ ability to make sense of sustainable consumption.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the knowledge-to-action gap is a result of the complexity of the marketplace and the discursive polyphonic nature of the marketplace.

the “knowledge-toaction” gap is partly due to the discursive polyphonic nature of the marketplace and the discursive struggles that consumers have to deal with in the context of their everyday consumption practices.
the knowledge-to-action gap in sustainable consumption is partly caused by discursive polyphony, which is a result of the discursive struggle over the meaning of sustainability.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

sustainable consumption is an ambiguous, contested concept and that consumers need to be aware that they are continuously exposed to different and partly clashing narratives on what sustainable consumption entails.
we have shown that the discursive complexity that consumers are confronted with is an important part of the explanation for the “knowledge-toaction” gap in sustainable consumption.
the knowledge-to-action gap can be attributed, at least partly, to the discursive polyphonic nature of sustainable consumption.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a discursive approach is useful for understanding the complexity of marketplace knowledge and the discursive struggle that is involved in making sense of sustainable development in everyday life.

the discursive confusion is not a problem in itself, but a consequence of the way in which sustainable consumption is framed in the marketplace, as it creates a discursive space for consumers to engage in and make sense of their role and responsibilities in sustainable consumption.

the consumer policy literature needs to pay more attention to the discursive nature of marketplace knowledge and the discursive polyphonies that consumers face when trying to make more sustainable consumption practices part of their daily lives.
